messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan was thirty-four, a firefighter in a mid-sized Midwestern city, married for seven years to a schoolteacher named Laura. Four years ago, he had volunteered for a two-month deployment as a civilian relief worker in a conflict zone—a decision he had made believing his emergency training would be useful. The specifics he still avoided revisiting: a convoy ambush near a checkpoint, then the chaotic aftermath of an explosion in a crowded market where he had helped pull bodies from debris. What stayed with him most was the moment when a local woman grabbed his arm, begging for help, and he had felt a surge of protective warmth—only to see her collapse seconds later from shrapnel wounds. That surge of positive emotion, he had since concluded, had made him less alert, more vulnerable. He had learned to push those feelings away immediately.

Back home, the routines of firefighting helped at first. But soon he noticed that even inside his own house, he was on guard. In the living room, he positioned his chair so that he could see both doorways. He would tense whenever a stranger approached him at the grocery store—a neighbor asking for directions felt like a potential threat. In every building, his eyes automatically scanned for exits; he had become so practiced that he noted the fire escape routes within seconds of entering a restaurant or a hardware store. His colleagues at the firehouse began to comment on his rigid posture during downtime.

The maladaptive strategies he adopted only made things worse. He stopped running—his longtime stress release—because the open streets felt exposed, full of unpredictable people. Without that outlet, his vigilance sharpened rather than softened. He developed a habit of sitting near any exit when he was out, and that very habit kept his focus locked on escape routes, which in turn kept his threat-detection system humming. At home, when Laura tried to hold his hand or laugh at a sitcom, he would deliberately flatten his mood. He would remind himself that feeling good was dangerous—it had been the moment he let his guard down in the war zone that had cost that woman her life. Pushing away positive emotions made him feel safer momentarily, but the emotional numbing left him more alone, more on edge, more convinced that the world was hostile. He began to monitor Laura’s movements too, feeling a spike of alarm if she walked up behind him unexpectedly.

These routines solidified over months. He stopped going to the gym altogether, which meant his physical tension had nowhere to go except to fuel his hypervigilance. At work, during a routine call to a house fire, he caught himself scanning the burning building’s exits rather than focusing on the hose line—a dangerous shift that his captain noticed and pulled him aside for. Ethan could not explain why the memory of a market half a world away felt more immediate than the flames in front of him.

What finally drove him to seek help was a sequence of small failures: he snapped at a stranger in a parking lot who merely walked too close; he missed a family dinner because he could not bring himself to sit in a booth that did not offer a clear escape path; he woke Laura at three in the morning because he had been lying still, eyes wide, checking every shadow. His marriage was beginning to strain, and he was terrified that his own hypervigilance was making him a hazard on the job. He wanted to stop feeling as though every stranger was a threat and every positive moment was a trap. But the thought of letting go of those strategies felt like stepping into an open field without cover—and that, more than anything, was what ached behind his eyes when he finally sat down in the therapist’s office.
